noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: be able to define first, second and third ionisation energies and understand that all ionisation energies are endothermic
understand how ionisation energies are influenced by the number of protons in the nucleus, the electron shielding and the sub-shell from which the electron is removed

primer.text: Removing an electron is never free. This note defines first, second and third ionisation energies on gaseous species with calcium's 590, 1145 and 4912 kJ mol-1 ladder, then bends the curve through its four factors: nuclear charge, distance, shielding and spin-pair repulsion.

lessons.title: Defining the ionisation ladder
lessons.opening: Every ionisation energy is an invoice for ripping one more electron from an ever more positive ion, and every invoice is paid in endothermic kJ mol^-1. This lesson defines first, second and third ionisation energies through calcium's 590, 1145 and 4912 values.
keyPoints: The first ionisation energy strips a mole of electrons from a mole of gaseous atoms, leaving gaseous 1+ ions.
Successive ionisation energies strip further electrons from ever more positive gaseous ions.
All ionisation energies are endothermic - energy must be supplied.
Calcium's IE1, IE2 and IE3 are +590, +1145 and +4912 kJ mol^-1.

low.restatement: IE1 strips the first electron from neutral gas atoms; IE2 and IE3 keep going, each costing more than the last.
low.analogy: It is peeling an onion while it grips tighter with every layer - each pull costs more effort.
low.examPointer: The gas-phase condition (g) is part of the definition - write it into equations like Ca (g) -> Ca+ (g) + e-.

medium.restatement: The definition counts one mole of each species under standard conditions (298 K, 101 kPa); the endothermic sign reflects overcoming nuclear attraction, which grows as ion charge rises.
medium.analogy: Removing electrons is like escaping gravity: each escape from a more positively charged body costs more fuel.
medium.examPointer: Quote the equation AND the value for calcium: Ca (g) -> Ca+ (g) + e-, IE1 = +590 kJ mol^-1.

check.stem: What does the first ionisation energy remove?

options.text: A mole of electrons leaving a mole of gaseous atoms, which become gaseous 1+ ions
options.explanation: The full definition names the amounts and the gaseous states.

options.text: One electron from the nucleus
options.explanation: Electrons are removed from orbitals, never the nucleus.

options.text: One mole of electrons from solid atoms
options.explanation: The definition requires the gaseous state.

options.text: Two moles of electrons per mole of atoms
options.explanation: IE1 removes exactly one electron per atom.

check.stem: Why are all ionisation energies endothermic?

options.text: Energy must be supplied to pull electrons away from the nucleus's attraction
options.explanation: Separation against attraction always absorbs energy.

options.text: Because electrons release energy when leaving
options.explanation: Leaving costs energy; falling in releases it.

options.text: Because the process happens at high temperature
options.explanation: The measurement conditions do not fix the sign.

options.text: Because ions are heavier than atoms
options.explanation: Removing electrons makes ions lighter.

check.stem: Calcium's IE2 is defined by which equation?

options.explanation: The second electron leaves the gaseous 1+ ion.

options.text: Ca (g) -> Ca+ (g) + e-
options.explanation: That is the first ionisation energy.
That is the third.

options.text: Ca (s) -> Ca+ (aq) + e-
options.explanation: Wrong state on both counts.

check.stem: Why is calcium's IE3 (+4912) far larger than its IE2 (+1145)?

options.text: The third electron comes from a principal shell closer to the nucleus (3p vs 4s)
options.explanation: The shell drop raises the attraction sharply.

options.text: Because calcium's nucleus gains a proton
options.explanation: The nucleus is unchanged during ionisation.

options.text: Because the ion becomes gaseous
options.explanation: It was gaseous already.

options.text: Because electrons repel the incoming energy
options.explanation: Repulsion plays no such role.

check.stem: Under which standard conditions are ionisation energies measured?

options.text: 298 K and 101 kPa, on gaseous atoms
options.explanation: The definition pins temperature and pressure.

options.text: 0 degrees C and 1 atmosphere
options.explanation: Those are s.t.p. conditions, not the IE standard.

options.text: 293 K and 101.3 kPa
options.explanation: That is r.t.p., used for gas volumes.

options.text: Whatever temperature the experiment uses
options.explanation: The standard set is part of the definition.

check.modelAnswer: It is the energy that strips a mole of electrons from a mole of gaseous 1+ ions, converting those ions into gaseous 2+ ions.

check.stem: State calcium's first, second and third ionisation energies.
check.modelAnswer: IE1 = +590 kJ mol^-1, IE2 = +1145 kJ mol^-1 and IE3 = +4912 kJ mol^-1, all endothermic.

check.stem: Explain why the ionisation energy sequence for one element always rises.
check.modelAnswer: Each removal leaves fewer electrons shielding a same-sized nucleus and increases the ion's positive charge, so the remaining electrons feel a stronger pull; the energy bill therefore climbs with every electron removed, with jumps at shell boundaries.

check.stem: Write the equation, with state symbols, for calcium's first ionisation energy and quote its value.
check.modelAnswer: Ca (g) -> Ca+ (g) + e- , IE1 = +590 kJ mol^-1; the gaseous states are part of the definition.

lessons.title: What bends the ionisation curve
lessons.opening: Ionisation energies are not arbitrary - four factors bend them: nuclear charge, distance, shielding and spin-pair repulsion. This lesson also fixes orbital capacities, so the sub-shell an electron leaves is part of the explanation.
keyPoints: Sub-shell capacities: s holds 2 electrons (1 orbital), p holds 6 (3 orbitals), d holds 10 (5), f holds 14 (7).
Bigger nuclear charge pulls electrons harder and raises IE.
Outer electrons farther away, or shielded by inner shells, are removed more easily.
Spin-pair repulsion makes paired electrons easier to remove than unpaired ones.

low.restatement: More protons raise the energy bill; more distance or more intervening shells lower it; paired electrons leave more willingly.
low.analogy: Pulling a magnet off a fridge: stronger magnet (charge), thicker cardboard (shielding) or greater reach (distance) all change the effort.
low.examPointer: Name all four factors when a question asks for influences - three of four is a standard partial mark.

medium.restatement: The four factors interact: nuclear charge sets the pull, distance attenuates it rapidly, inner shells screen it, and within a sub-shell an already-paired electron repels its partner - which is why group 1 metals ionise easily and noble gases resist.
medium.analogy: The outer electron is an audience member deciding whether to leave a concert: the band's pull (charge), seat row (distance), the crowd in between (shielding) and an elbowing neighbour (pair repulsion) all tip the decision.
medium.examPointer: Link periodicity: low IE for group 1, very high for noble gases - evidence of the configuration dependence.

check.stem: How many orbitals does a p sub-shell contain, and what total does that permit?

options.text: Three orbitals, holding six electrons in total
options.explanation: Each orbital takes two electrons of opposite spin: 3 x 2 = 6.

options.text: One orbital holding two electrons
options.explanation: That describes an s sub-shell.

options.text: Five orbitals holding ten
options.explanation: That describes a d sub-shell.

options.text: Three orbitals holding three
options.explanation: Each orbital holds TWO electrons.

check.stem: Increasing nuclear charge across a period has what effect on first ionisation energy?

options.text: It raises IE, because more protons attract the outer electrons more strongly
options.explanation: The pull grows with the proton count.

options.text: It lowers IE, because atoms get heavier
options.explanation: Mass does not set the pull.

options.text: It has no effect until a shell fills
options.explanation: The effect is continuous across the period.

options.text: It first raises then lowers IE
options.explanation: The general trend rises across a period.

check.stem: Why does increased shielding make the outer electron easier to remove?

options.text: Inner-shell electrons screen the outer electron from the nucleus's full attraction
options.explanation: The net pull the outer electron feels is reduced.

options.text: Because shielding adds protons
options.explanation: Shielding adds no protons.

options.text: Because the outer electron pairs up
options.explanation: Pairing is a separate factor.

options.text: Because shields reduce distance
options.explanation: Shielding acts between distance and charge.

check.stem: What is spin-pair repulsion and what does it cause?

options.text: Two electrons sharing an orbital repel slightly, so paired electrons are removed more easily
options.explanation: The pairing offsets nuclear attraction.

options.text: Opposite spins attract, stabilising pairs
options.explanation: Repulsion, not attraction, characterises the pair.

options.text: It only affects noble gases
options.explanation: It operates wherever electrons pair.

options.text: It raises ionisation energy for pairs
options.explanation: It LOWERS the energy needed.

check.stem: Why do noble gases show very high ionisation energies while group 1 metals show low ones?

options.text: Noble gases hold full sub-shells with strong, unshielded nuclear pull on outer electrons; group 1 metals have a single, shielded, easily lost electron
options.explanation: Configuration decides the bill.

options.text: Because noble gases are heavier
options.explanation: Mass is not the driver.

options.text: Because group 1 metals are gases
options.explanation: They are metals.

options.text: Because noble gases carry charge
options.explanation: They are neutral atoms.

check.stem: State the orbital count and electron capacity of s, p and d sub-shells.
check.modelAnswer: s holds one orbital (2 electrons), p holds three orbitals (6 electrons) and d holds five orbitals (10 electrons).

check.stem: State the four factors affecting the size of a first ionisation energy.
check.modelAnswer: Nuclear charge, distance of the outer electrons from the nucleus, shielding by inner electrons, and spin-pair repulsion.

check.stem: Explain why attraction falls off rapidly with distance and why that matters for large atoms.
check.modelAnswer: Electrostatic attraction weakens steeply as separation grows, so an outer electron two shells further out feels dramatically less pull; that is why large atoms with many inner shells lose their outer electrons at low energies compared with compact atoms of the same group.

check.stem: Predict, with reasons, which loses an electron more easily: a lithium 2s electron or a helium 1s electron.
check.modelAnswer: Lithium's 2s electron: it sits farther from the nucleus and is shielded by the 1s pair, so it is removed far more easily than helium's unshielded, close-in 1s electron.

glossary.definition: The energy that converts a mole of gaseous atoms into gaseous 1+ ions by stripping a mole of electrons.
The slight repulsion between two electrons sharing an orbital, making paired electrons easier to remove.
The screening of nuclear attraction experienced by outer electrons due to inner-shell electrons.
